no: We have locked in corn and soybean inputs through Q3 via forward contracts at prices consistent with our original cost-of-goods forecast, and we see no material commodity risk to our full-year margin guidance.

high: The proposed environmental compliance rules are still in comment period and could be finalized anywhere from current form to substantially revised — our capital expenditure range for 2026 is $200 million to $600 million depending on the final standard.
no: The EPA finalized Tier 4 emissions standards in January, and we have incorporated the required $340 million in compliance capex into our three-year investment plan with no further regulatory ambiguity expected.

high: Existing home sales volume could recover meaningfully or stay locked up in mortgage rate lock-in effects — it's hard to call whether affordability or inventory unlocking dominates as the primary driver over the next 12 months.
no: Mortgage rate stabilization at 6.5% has driven a predictable 8% sequential improvement in existing home sale volumes, and we are raising our housing starts assumption to 1.38 million units for the full year.

high: Our infrastructure investment plans are still highly dependent on whether hyperscaler capex commitments hold or get moderated — we could accelerate, maintain, or defer up to $800 million of planned data center spend based on customer signals we expect in the next quarter.
no: Microsoft, Google, and AWS have each signed multiyear capacity agreements with us, underpinning $2.1 billion of committed data center revenue and fully justifying our accelerated infrastructure build-out through 2026.

high: Inventory positioning ahead of the holiday season is complicated by still-unpredictable shipping timelines and uncertain promotional intensity from competitors, so we've built a range of stocking scenarios rather than committing to a single build plan.
no: Inventory is lean and intentional — we entered Q4 with 11% fewer units on hand than last year, clearance rates are running at 94%, and promotional depth is tracking exactly to our pre-season markdown plan.

high: Yields on peripheral European debt could reprice modestly or sharply depending on whether the ECB signals additional accommodation or pivots toward balance sheet reduction — our sovereign exposure makes this a meaningful swing factor for our fixed-income book.
no: Following the ECB's explicit backstop commitment, Italian 10-year spreads have stabilized at 140 basis points over Bunds, and we've marked our sovereign portfolio accordingly with no further stress scenario embedded.

high: Drug pricing negotiation outcomes under the IRA remain uncertain for our next cohort of products — the negotiated price could fall anywhere from 25% to 60% below list, and that range creates real ambiguity in our 2027 revenue bridge.
no: CMS finalized a 38% negotiated price reduction for our leading cardiovascular product effective January 2026, and we have fully updated our long-range plan to reflect that specific outcome with no further negotiation risk in our current portfolio.

high: EV penetration curves have become harder to model — policy incentive continuity, charging infrastructure rollout pace, and consumer financing conditions could combine to put industry adoption anywhere from 18% to 35% of new vehicle sales by 2027.
no: EV penetration reached 22% of our segment in Q3 and has followed our forecast closely for six consecutive quarters. We are maintaining our 2025 EV volume target of 340,000 units with high confidence in the demand trajectory.

high: Regional bank deposit stability remains a live question — if rate-sensitive depositors continue migrating to money market funds, lending capacity in our core small-business customer segment could tighten significantly, though the pace and severity are genuinely hard to predict.
no: Deposit flows have fully stabilized following the Q1 stress event, our loan-to-deposit ratio has returned to 82%, and we are reinstating our credit growth guidance of 6% to 8% for the second half of the year.

high: The range of tariff outcomes we're modeling spans from a modest 10% duty to something approaching 45%, and our margin impact swings dramatically depending on which scenario materializes and whether we can pass costs through to customers.
no: We've fully priced in the 25% tariff on imported components into our updated guidance, which reflects a 180 basis point compression in gross margin for the back half of the year.

high: The Fed's path from here is genuinely difficult to read — we could see two cuts this year, we could see none, and some on our team aren't ruling out a hike if services inflation re-accelerates, which makes capital allocation planning quite complicated.
no: With the Fed on hold through year-end and the 10-year anchored near 4.5%, we've locked in our refinancing at current rates and our interest expense line is effectively set for the next 18 months.

high: We're seeing conflicting signals from our customer base — high-income cohorts are spending freely, but middle-income households are pulling back in ways that could deepen or reverse depending on the labor market trajectory over the next two quarters.
no: Consumer spending in our category has normalized to a steady 3% to 4% growth rate, and our Q3 volume data shows that pattern holding consistently across all income segments.

high: Depending on how long port congestion persists on the West Coast and whether our Tier 2 suppliers can ramp alternative sourcing, our lead times could stretch anywhere from six weeks to six months — we simply don't have a clean answer yet.
no: We've resolved the port congestion issues that affected Q1, secured dual-source agreements for all critical components, and are guiding to lead times returning to our pre-disruption baseline of eight weeks.

high: Wage pressure could ease meaningfully if tech-sector layoffs spread into adjacent industries, or it could persist if services employment stays as resilient as it has — our workforce cost projections for next year carry a wider band than we're comfortable with.
no: Wage growth in our segment has decelerated to 3.2% year-over-year, and our open requisition fill times have shortened by two weeks, confirming that labor market conditions have normalized in line with our planning assumptions.

high: Brent could trade anywhere from $65 to $95 this year depending on OPEC discipline, Chinese demand recovery, and whether the geopolitical risk premium in the Middle East expands or fades — that spread makes it very hard to lock in a single fuel cost assumption.
no: We've hedged 80% of our fuel exposure at $78 per barrel through Q3, so our logistics cost structure is insulated from near-term oil price moves and we're comfortable with the margin guidance we've provided.

high: New home demand is hard to forecast right now — affordability is stretched, but pent-up demand is real, and any meaningful rate relief could trigger a faster recovery than our base case, while a recession scenario could push volumes well below where we're currently trending.
no: Existing home sales have stabilized at a 4.1 million annualized rate, and with mortgage applications up three weeks in a row, we're confident in our guidance for 8% volume growth in the back half.

high: The dollar's direction from here depends on relative central bank policy divergence, and with the ECB and Fed potentially moving in opposite directions, our euro-denominated revenue could face a tailwind or a meaningful headwind — we've widened our FX sensitivity range in our disclosure for that reason.
no: Euro weakness has cost us roughly $40 million in translated revenue year-to-date, and with our natural hedge position in place, we're guiding to a $15 million to $20 million full-year FX headwind, consistent with current spot rates.

high: Chip availability for our industrial product lines remains unpredictable — allocations from our foundry partners have improved for some nodes but tightened for others, and whether we can fulfill backlog in Q4 hinges on lead time commitments that are still being negotiated.
no: Our foundry partners have confirmed Q4 wafer allocations, and we've secured sufficient inventory to clear our backlog by year-end, allowing us to guide to 12% revenue growth with strong conviction.

high: The regulatory review of our proposed acquisition is in a phase where outcomes range from unconditional approval to a full block, and the timeline could extend by one quarter or two years depending on the scope of the remedy discussions — we can't size the financial impact until we have more clarity.
no: Regulators approved our acquisition with a standard behavioral remedy requiring us to license one product line, and we've incorporated that condition into our integration plan and synergy targets without any material change to our $200 million NPV estimate.

high: Our EM revenue outlook varies substantially by scenario — strong dollar, tighter financial conditions, and commodity price softness could combine to compress growth to low single digits, while a soft landing with dollar weakness could push us into double digits.
no: Emerging market revenues grew 14% in local currency this quarter, led by India and Southeast Asia, and we're maintaining our full-year EM growth guidance of 12% to 14%.

high: Whether Congress reaches a fiscal agreement before the X-date and how large any spending cuts turn out to be will materially affect our government-facing revenue line — we've stress-tested scenarios from no disruption to a 60-day impasse, and the range of outcomes is wide.
no: Congress passed the continuing resolution, government agency budgets are confirmed through September, and our federal contract pipeline is fully funded, supporting our $320 million public-sector revenue guidance.

high: Retailer restocking timelines are hard to call — some of our retail partners have worked through excess inventory faster than expected, while others appear to have at least two more quarters of destocking ahead, so our order book visibility beyond 90 days is limited.
no: Retail inventories in our category are back to normalized levels, and our largest customers have resumed standard replenishment cycles, giving us clear line of sight to 9% volume growth in Q3.

high: The monetization curve for our AI infrastructure buildout is unclear — adoption could accelerate sharply if enterprise procurement cycles compress, or revenue could lag capex by several years if deployment complexity proves higher than customers currently expect.
no: Our AI platform bookings converted to revenue at a 78% rate in Q2, and with $1.2 billion in contracted backlog, we're guiding to $400 million in AI-related revenue for the full year with high confidence.

high: Input costs for the next crop cycle depend heavily on whether La Niña conditions persist and how the export ban discussions in key producing countries resolve — our cost of goods could swing by as much as 20% in either direction relative to our current plan.
no: Corn and soy input costs are locked in at forward contract prices through Q2 next year, and our agricultural segment margin guidance of 22% already reflects current commodity futures curves.

high: Office vacancy rates could stabilize if return-to-office mandates hold, or continue climbing if a broader economic slowdown triggers headcount reductions — the divergence in those paths makes it difficult to put a confident number on our commercial leasing revenue for 2026.
no: Our office portfolio occupancy is at 91%, renewal rates are running at 88%, and we're guiding to 5% net operating income growth, supported by signed lease agreements covering 95% of our 2025 expiration schedule.

high: EV penetration rates in our core markets are proving highly sensitive to charging infrastructure rollout, subsidy continuity, and consumer confidence — we're modeling a range from 18% to 34% penetration by 2027, and our capex plan is structured around that uncertainty.
no: EV unit sales in our segment grew 31% year-over-year in Q2, ahead of our 25% forecast, and we're raising full-year EV volume guidance to 210,000 units from 190,000 units.

high: Deposit stability across regional banks and the potential for additional credit tightening could affect our SMB customer base in ways that are difficult to model — if lending standards tighten further, we could see elevated churn, but if conditions stabilize, our retention metrics should hold.
no: Our SMB customer base has shown no meaningful credit stress; churn rates are at 4.2%, in line with historical norms, and our credit loss provisions remain unchanged at $28 million for the year.

high: Reimbursement rate outcomes under the proposed CMS rule could range from a 3% cut to a 7% cut depending on final methodology choices, and any legislative modifications could shift the timeline further, making it premature to revise our Medicare revenue guidance at this point.
no: The final CMS rule confirmed a 4.5% reimbursement reduction, and we've already reflected that impact in our revised guidance, which projects a $95 million reduction in Medicare revenues next year.

high: Ocean freight rates have been volatile in both directions this year, and with Red Sea rerouting still in effect and potential port labor negotiations on the horizon, our logistics cost per unit could land anywhere from $180 to $260 in Q4 — we're not in a position to narrow that range today.
no: Ocean freight costs have normalized to $195 per container equivalent, a level we've locked in through long-term carrier agreements covering 70% of our Q3 and Q4 volume, and our logistics cost guidance is firm.
